description:
Why should someone join a Space Mission Design Game?

1. Explore the world of space exploration

2. Develop problem-solving and critical-thinking skills

3. Build teamwork and collaboration

4. Learn science, technology, and engineering

5. Explore artificial intelligence and innovation
summary:
Orbital Space Run is an interactive, browser-based game series designed to introduce players to the exciting world of rocket missions and space exploration. It features four difficulty levels: Beginner, Intermediate, Advanced, and Master, all accessible through one space-themed launcher.
Each level offers a unique mission and learning experience. In Beginner mode, players build a spacecraft, accept contracts, and manage a crew. Intermediate mode introduces orbital mechanics and delta-v as players navigate missions from Earth to the Moon. Advanced mode provides hands-on flight control, including throttle management, booster separation, parachutes, and oxygen systems. Master mode challenges players to manage a complete $100 million space program, balancing budgets, spacecraft components, fuel, life support, mass, and thrust.
The game gradually introduces real-world spaceflight concepts through interactive challenges, encouraging critical thinking, problem-solving, and engineering skills. All four games are combined into a single file that runs on computers without requiring accounts, downloads, or sign-ins. It is completely free and suitable for classrooms, families, and students.
If the game does not start automatically, download the file and open it using a web browser such as Google Chrome.
details:
What it does and how it works

Orbital Space Run is a four-level spaceflight game series behind one launcher. Players press START on the title screen, then pick Beginner, Intermediate, Advanced or Master. Each level shows a short mission briefing and a second START button that opens its game.

  • Beginner: Players run a small space program. They build a ship, take contracts and buy supplies so the crew survives the mission.
  • Intermediate: Players fly missions from the launch pad to the lunar surface using real orbital mechanics, managing delta-v and a mission budget.
  • Advanced (Ascent: Rocket Missions): Players fly the rocket themselves. They control throttle, booster separation and parachutes, and land on target while watching oxygen, water and food.
  • Master: A full launch-program simulator. Players design a vehicle from a parts catalog within a $100 million budget, balancing propellant, life support, mass, thrust and delta-v.

A Menu button returns players to the level select at any time. Progress and credits save in the player’s browser.

Benefits

  • It’s free and works on computers.
  • There are no accounts, downloads or sign-ins. The whole game is one file that can be emailed, put on a USB stick or hosted anywhere.
  • The difficulty climbs gradually, so younger or newer players can start simple and advanced players still get a real challenge.

Intended impact

We want students, families and classrooms to learn by doing. Instead of reading about mass, thrust and fuel, players feel why those trade-offs matter when a mission succeeds or fails. We hope it sparks interest in science, engineering and space careers, especially for kids who don’t have access to space programs or expensive software.

Tools, languages and software

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
  • Graphics: HTML Canvas for the animated starfield and SVG for the rocket artwork.
  • Fonts: Google Fonts.
  • AI: We used Claude, Anthropic’s AI assistant, to help build and refine the games and the launcher.
  • Bundling and testing: A Python script packed all four games into one file. We used Playwright to test each level.
  • Hardware: No special hardware is needed. It runs in any modern web browser.

What makes it creative

Rather than one game with a difficulty slider, each level is a different kind of game: program management at Beginner, physics flight at Intermediate, hands-on piloting at Advanced and full engineering design at Master. Together they cover the main parts of a real space mission. The arcade-style title screen and mission briefings make it feel like joining a space program and earning your way up the ranks.

Factors we considered

  • Accessibility: Large tap targets, a layout that fits phones and readable text. The animation turns off for players who set their device to reduce motion.
  • Easy access: We packed everything into one file after players were asked to sign in to play, so nobody needs an account.
  • Learning curve: We ordered the levels so each one builds on skills from the one before.
  • Accuracy and fun together: We kept real spaceflight ideas while keeping the controls simple enough to pick up quickly.
  • Offline use: It works offline for schools or homes with poor internet. Only the fonts need a connection.
